name: Justice Defenders
mission: JUSTICE DEFENDERS PROVIDES LEGAL EDUCATION, TRAINING, AND PRACTICE WITHIN DEFENSELESS COMMUNITIES. FOUNDED IN 2007, JUSTICE DEFENDERS WORK ACROSS 35+ PRISONS IN AFRICA WHERE INCARCERATED PEOPLE AND OFFICERS TRAIN AND PROVIDE LEGAL SERVICES FOR THEMSELVES AND OTHERS.
theoryOfChange: Justice Defenders has a published Theory of Change as part of 'The Justice Defenders Way' document on their website. This framework outlines their approach to transforming justice systems. Their 2025-2027 strategy focuses on growing their movement by expanding legal education and practice, creating new pathways from incarceration to advocacy, and advancing relational systems change to restore trust across justice institutions. They aim to serve 100,000 clients with free legal advice across East Africa and the United States, establish 10 new prison communities (including one in the United States), and file 10 public interest litigation petitions to challenge unconstitutional laws.

rich_narrative.summary: Justice Defenders is a unique legal advocacy organization that works within the African prison system. founded in 2007, the charity <cite id="1">trains incarcerated people and prison staff as paralegals</cite> to provide legal services to those who cannot afford a lawyer. The organization focuses on <cite id="2">legal education, training, and practice</cite> to ensure fair hearings for defenseless communities. While the charity maintains a <cite id="3">Platinum Seal of Transparency from Candid</cite>, its financial profile shows recent contraction. In FY2023, the organization reported <cite id="4">total revenue of $1,868,837</cite>, which represents a <cite id="5">significant decline from the $6.3 million reported in 2022</cite>. Despite this volatility, the charity has achieved notable outcomes, including <cite id="6">facilitating the release of 12,870 clients</cite> according to their most recent reporting. The model relies on <cite id="7">capacity building through prison legal offices</cite> in countries like Kenya and Uganda. However, donors should note that the <cite id="8">program expense ratio is 58.5%</cite>, which is below the 75% sector benchmark. This reflects a high proportion of spending on administrative and fundraising costs compared to direct service delivery. The charity remains a <cite id="9">Sadaqah-eligible option</cite> for donors interested in systemic justice reform and human rights within Muslim-majority regions of Africa.
